record.paper_title: KAM theorems and open problems for infinite dimensional Hamiltonian with short range
record.context_brief: Dense pure point spectrum with non-short-range nonlinearity
record.original_question: Consider a Hamiltonian system whose linearized operator, for example -Delta_f + v, has pure point spectrum and a part of that spectrum is dense in a finite interval. If the nonlinear part of the Hamiltonian is not short range, as can occur for partial differential equations on the whole space, do KAM tori exist for the system?

evidence.quote: Here is no any conditions imposed on the normal frequencies lambda_n's, except that which are of pure point spectra and are non-zero. Therefore, these frequencies can densely distributed on an finite interval. For example, they can be all rational number in the interval [1,2].

Problem 2. Assume that the linearized operator (-Delta_f +v, for example,) of a hamiltonian system is of pure point spectra, part of which is dense in some finite interval, and assume that the nonlinear part of the Hamiltonian is not of short rang (in partial differential equations defined in the whole space, for example). Are there any KAM tori for the system? This problem is apparently open.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system whose phase space consists of real-valued functions (or pairs of canonically conjugate variables) on an unbounded spatial domain such as $\mathbb{R}^d$. Suppose the Hamiltonian has the form
$$H = H_0 + P,$$
where the linearized (quadratic) part $H_0$ is associated with a self-adjoint operator $L = -\Delta + v(x)$ (with $v$ a real potential) whose spectrum is purely point spectrum $\{\lambda_n\}_{n\ge 1}$, with all $\lambda_n \neq 0$, and such that a subset of the eigenvalues $\{\lambda_n\}$ is dense in some non-degenerate finite interval $[a,b] \subset \mathbb{R}$ (for instance, all rationals in $[1,2]$). Assume further that the nonlinear perturbation $P$ is not of short range: when expanded in the eigenbasis $\{\phi_n\}$ of $L$, the coupling coefficients between modes do not decay sufficiently fast with the difference of indices to satisfy the standard short-range (exponential/off-diagonal decay) assumptions used in infinite-dimensional KAM theory; this situation naturally arises for nonlinear PDEs posed on the whole space $\mathbb{R}^d$.

Question: Under these hypotheses, do there exist KAM (quasi-periodic invariant) tori for the Hamiltonian system generated by $H$? Equivalently, does there exist a positive-measure (or at least non-empty) set of frequency vectors for which the unperturbed quasi-periodic motions of $H_0$ persist as invariant tori of the full system $H_0 + P$?
artifact.status_search_result: A web search indicates that infinite-dimensional KAM results for Hamiltonian PDEs typically require either compact spatial domains (giving discrete, non-dense spectrum) or short-range/off-diagonal-decay structure on the nonlinearity (as in Pöschel's full-dimensional tori results). No results were found establishing KAM tori in the combined regime of dense pure point spectrum together with non-short-range nonlinearity on the whole space; the problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Maximal tori in infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian systems: a Renormalization Group approach
status_evidence.snippet: Pöschel proved the existence of full dimensional tori for infinite dimensional Hamiltonian systems with spatial structure of short range couplings.
status_evidence.claim: Existing full-dimensional KAM results rely on short-range coupling assumptions, which are violated in the setting of the problem.

status_evidence.title: Infinite dimensional invariant tori for nonlinear Schrödinger equations
status_evidence.snippet: KAM results for NLS are formulated on the torus with discrete spectrum and decay/short-range conditions on the perturbation.
status_evidence.claim: Standard KAM frameworks for nonlinear Schrödinger equations assume compact domains and short-range structure, not the whole-space setting with dense point spectrum.
